cases.answer: Compare them as different measures in different populations, not as directly comparable risk estimates. Helsinki reported an absolute frequency of grade 1–2 myocarditis: 11 of 75 patients (14.7%) receiving pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant therapy for early TNBC in a retrospective cohort. Adverse events were collected throughout neoadjuvant therapy and for 30 days after pembrolizumab discontinuation, with troponin measured before every pembrolizumab cycle. The lung-cancer RCT meta-analysis reported relative risks of any cardiac adverse event versus chemotherapy: RR 2.15 (95% CI 1.13–4.12) for single ICI and RR 1.38 (1.05–1.82) for single ICI plus chemotherapy. Its median follow-up was 18.1 months. Its myocarditis-specific estimate was RR 1.67 (0.67–4.16) versus placebo or chemotherapy, which was not statistically significant. Differences in cancer population, endpoint, study design, surveillance and observation period limit direct comparison; the meta-analysis also warns that some trials reported only severe cardiovascular events.

cases.answer: No. The review explicitly says that blood-based MCED has not demonstrated a mortality benefit. It identifies LDCT as the only lung-cancer screening modality with demonstrated mortality benefit, citing a 20% relative reduction in lung-cancer mortality versus chest radiography in the National Lung Screening Trial. MCED's analytical feasibility and increased early-stage detection do not establish an equivalent mortality benefit; the review says NHS-Galleri missed its primary endpoint of reducing combined stage III–IV cancers.

cases.answer: No. The cited HP2030 values—84.3% for cervical screening and 74.4% for colorectal screening—are recommended goals for each cancer individually, not Harper's achieved study rates. The study analyzed 40,511 women aged 50–64 with complete screening data in the 2018 BRFSS survey and reported a weighted dual-screening prevalence of 58.2% (95% CI 57.1–59.4). Its Results section gives traditional individual screening rates of 86% (85.4–86.1) for cervical cancer and 66% (65.9–66.8) for colorectal cancer. There is an internal discrepancy: Figure 1 and the eLife digest give colorectal screening as 64%, rather than the Results section's 66%.
